claims.text: A multi-fidelity machine-learning framework can tune the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior of non-equiatomic HEAs.
Machine-learning-guided selection of composition and processing parameters can optimize local magnetic ordering.
Non-equiatomic HEA thin films or nanostructures possess inherent compositional heterogeneity.
Non-equiatomic HEA thin films or nanostructures have complex local magnetic interactions.
A framework trained on experimental and computational data can predict correlations among composition, microstructure, and magnetic properties.
Model predictions can be used to adjust HEA compositions and processing conditions.
Controlled thermal and magnetic fields permit characterization of magnetic transitions and magnetocaloric responses in low-dimensional systems.
Localized magnetic ordering mediates the overall magnetocaloric response.
Phase fractions or domain structures mediate the overall magnetocaloric response.
HEAs have a vast compositional design space that motivates advanced and efficient design tools.
Machine learning can identify non-obvious correlations within the compositional space of non-equiatomic HEAs.
Targeted compositional and processing adjustments enhance local magnetic interactions.
Enhanced local magnetic interactions improve the magnetocaloric effect by optimizing magnetic entropy changes near the transition.
The proposed method can produce a larger magnetic entropy change or more precise control of the transition temperature than equiatomic alloying or conventional thermal treatment.
Equiatomic compositions and standard thermal treatments provide limited control over magnetic transitions in low-dimensional HEAs.
Traditional tuning methods have lower magnetocaloric performance than the proposed machine-learning approach.
The approach should be most effective in thin films or nanostructures because local magnetic ordering can be distinctly manipulated there.
There is limited prior experimental validation of multi-fidelity machine learning for non-equiatomic, low-dimensional magnetocaloric HEAs.
Integrating multi-fidelity data may have difficulty converging on optimal alloy and processing parameters.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, such as at least a 20% magnetocaloric enhancement or a measurable transition-temperature shift, would falsify the hypothesis.
